events.description: ANZ's monthly survey of New Zealand business sentiment. July's reading jumped to 56.1, its strongest level since February, with exporters, investment and employment intentions all firmer. A useful, if noisy, early read on how firms are feeling ahead of the harder activity data.

A monthly measure of the volume of goods sold by retailers in the Eurozone's largest economy. Since German consumer spending accounts for a big share of Eurozone demand, a surprise here can move the euro ahead of the bloc wide growth and inflation figures due later the same morning.

An early estimate of quarterly economic growth in Germany, the Eurozone's largest economy. This morning's preliminary print came in at 0.2% quarter on quarter, ahead of the 0.1% consensus though still slower than Q1's 0.3% pace, with exports doing the heavy lifting while consumer spending stayed subdued. Often moves the euro ahead of the full Eurozone GDP figure released later the same morning.

events.revisedNote: Corrected from the previous update, which had placed this release on Friday 31 July with a June comparison figure of 101.2. The KOF Swiss Economic Institute confirmed the barometer was actually published this morning, Thursday 30 July, with June's reading standing at 102.1. The July figure came in at 103.5, comfortably above the 100.7 consensus and the highest level since February.
events.description: A monthly composite leading indicator for the Swiss economy from the KOF Swiss Economic Institute, pointing to likely activity over the next six months. Today's better than expected reading, driven by broad based improvement across manufacturing, construction and services, reinforces signs that Switzerland's recovery is gaining traction, though it typically moves the franc less than a central bank event would.

events.revisedNote: Q1 growth has been revised up to flat from the previously reported 0.2% contraction, and this morning's Q2 flash estimate surprised to the upside at +0.4% quarter on quarter, well above the roughly 0.2% consensus that had been pencilled in.
events.description: An early estimate of quarterly economic growth across the whole Eurozone. One of the most closely watched growth indicators for the euro, feeding directly into the ECB's outlook for the bloc; today's print came in well ahead of expectations, easing fears of a second straight weak quarter.
A public appearance by Philip Lane, the ECB's Chief Economist. His remarks are watched closely as he is seen as a bellwether for the Governing Council's internal thinking on inflation and growth.

events.event: Bank of England interest rate decision
events.description: The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee announces its decision on Bank Rate, the UK's main interest rate. The Bank held at 3.75% for a fifth consecutive meeting, matching consensus, after a bigger than expected drop in inflation last month gave the Committee room to look through the market volatility caused by renewed fighting in Iran. Alongside the decision the Bank published its quarterly Monetary Policy Report and the minutes recording how each member voted.

events.event: BoE Monetary Policy Report & Financial Stability Report
events.description: Published alongside the rate decision, this sets out the Bank's updated forecasts for inflation and growth, plus its assessment of risks to the UK financial system. Markets read this closely for clues on the future path of rates.

events.event: BoE National MPC Agency briefing (Huw Pill and Fergal Shortall)
events.description: A briefing from Chief Economist Huw Pill and Fergal Shortall, head of the BoE's Agency network, held straight after the rate decision. Focuses on regional business conditions feeding into the MPC's thinking; a secondary event compared with the Governor's press conference.

Governor Andrew Bailey takes questions from journalists straight after the rate decision. Often the moment that moves sterling most, since this is where the Bank explains its reasoning in its own words, including how it is weighing the inflation undershoot against the risks from the wider geopolitical backdrop.

An early estimate of German inflation, released ahead of the full Eurozone inflation figure the following day. Economists expect a pick up from June's 2.3% as a temporary fuel duty cut expires. As the bloc's largest economy, Germany's number often sets the tone for how the euro reacts to the Eurozone print.

events.revisedNote: The advance estimate landed well short of forecasts: real GDP grew at an annualized 1.5% in Q2, versus the 2.3% consensus and down from Q1's 2.1% pace. The Bureau of Economic Analysis attributed the slowdown to softer consumer spending and investment, partly offset by a smaller drag from government spending.
events.description: The first official estimate of US economic growth for the quarter. A core input into how the Fed and markets judge the health of the world's largest economy: today's sizeable miss is likely to feed the debate over whether the Fed's hold this week left policy too tight, and has weighed on the dollar.

The Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, the Federal Reserve's preferred measure of inflation. Today's reading came in exactly in line with consensus at 3.3% year on year, with the quarterly core rate easing to 3.4% from 4.4% in Q1. Confirms inflation is cooling gradually rather than sharply, keeping the Fed on a cautious, data dependent footing.

events.revisedNote: The prior week's reading was revised up slightly to 188,000 from the previously reported 187,000. This week's claims (for the period to 25 July) rose 9,000 to 197,000, coming in below the 200,000 consensus and pointing to a still resilient, if gradually cooling, labour market.
events.description: The number of people filing for unemployment benefits for the first time that week. A high frequency, early read on the US labour market; usually a minor mover unless it deviates sharply from expectations, though today's release lands alongside the GDP and PCE data for extra scrutiny.

The share of Japan's labour force out of work. Japan's jobless rate has stayed extremely low for years, so this is rarely a big yen mover, but it feeds into the Bank of Japan's broader assessment of wage and price pressure ahead of tomorrow's policy decision.

events.event: Japan retail sales and industrial production (June)
events.previous: 1.9% m/m retail sales, 0.1% m/m industrial production (May)
events.consensus: -1.5% m/m retail sales, -0.5% m/m industrial production
events.description: Monthly gauges of Japanese household spending and factory output. Together they give an early steer on how the economy is tracking into the third quarter, and are watched by the BoJ for signs of whether domestic demand can support further policy normalisation.

Inflation data for Tokyo, published about three weeks ahead of the nationwide figure and widely used as a leading indicator for Japan wide price pressure. Released hours after the Bank of Japan's own decision, it can shift expectations for future rate hikes and move the yen.

events.event: China NBS Manufacturing and Non-Manufacturing PMI (July)
events.description: China's official, government compiled gauges of manufacturing and services and construction activity, released on the last day of the month. A reading above 50 signals expansion; below signals contraction. Among the more closely watched early signals of Chinese economic health, which matters for AUD and NZD as much as CNY given trade links.

The Australian Bureau of Statistics' quarterly measure of price changes faced by producers before they reach consumers. A slower moving gauge than the CPI, but one the RBA watches for early signs of cost pressures building up through supply chains, particularly relevant given the Bank's recent focus on upside inflation risks.

events.event: Bank of Japan interest rate decision
events.description: The Bank of Japan announces its target for short term interest rates alongside its quarterly Outlook Report. The BoJ is expected to hold today, but with the yen trading near multi decade lows, markets will focus on whether the report's growth outlook points to the next hike landing in October or December.

Governor Kazuo Ueda explains the decision and answers questions from the press. Often moves the yen more than the decision itself, particularly any comments on the pace of further policy normalisation and the timing of the next hike.

events.event: SARB Governor Kganyago speaks at Reserve Bank AGM
events.description: Governor Lesetja Kganyago addresses the South African Reserve Bank's 106th Ordinary Annual General Meeting of shareholders. As the SARB's chief policymaker, his remarks on inflation and the rand are watched for signals ahead of the next Monetary Policy Committee meeting in September.

An early estimate of Eurozone wide inflation for the month. One of the key inputs into the ECB's interest rate decisions and a regular source of euro volatility on release; today's expected rebound is being driven mainly by higher energy prices, while core inflation is seen holding near 2.4%.
The percentage of the Eurozone workforce that is unemployed. A slower moving indicator that rarely surprises markets, but still forms part of the broader picture of Eurozone economic health.

events.event: Canada GDP by industry (May, with June advance estimate)
events.description: Statistics Canada's monthly measure of economic output by industry. Released with a roughly two month lag, it gives an early read on how the Canadian economy is tracking heading into the third quarter.
A regional survey of purchasing managers in the Chicago area, used as an early signal for the following week's national ISM manufacturing survey. Usually a modest, secondary market mover.

A private sector survey of Chinese manufacturing activity, skewed toward smaller, export and tech oriented firms, released a few days after the official NBS PMI. Often diverges from the official gauge and is watched as a cross check on the health of China's factory sector, with knock on relevance for AUD and NZD.

A survey of purchasing managers in South Africa's manufacturing sector, compiled by Absa and the Bureau for Economic Research and usually published on the first business day of the month. A reading above 50 signals expansion; a below consensus print tends to weigh on the rand given the sector's fragile recent run.

Switzerland's headline inflation reading from the Federal Statistical Office. With Swiss inflation running well below other major economies, this feeds directly into the SNB's assessment of whether its current policy stance remains appropriate.

The final, revised reading of S&P Global's Eurozone manufacturing survey, usually only a small adjustment from the flash estimate published earlier in the month. A confirmation style release that rarely moves the euro much on its own.
The final, revised reading of S&P Global's UK manufacturing survey. Like its Eurozone counterpart, this is usually a modest revision to the flash figure and a secondary mover for sterling.

The Institute for Supply Management's survey of US manufacturing activity, released on the first business day of the month. A reading above 50 signals expansion. Watched as an early, broad based signal of US industrial health for the month just ended, and takes on extra weight this week following Thursday's weak GDP print.

The British Retail Consortium's monthly gauge of average shop prices, published around ten days ahead of the official ONS inflation figures. A useful early steer on the direction of UK consumer price pressure, though it rarely moves sterling much on its own.

S&P Global's survey of activity in the UK construction sector. Housebuilding has been the weakest part of the industry recently, so this is watched for signs of whether that drag is easing; typically a minor mover for sterling.

Statistics Canada's monthly snapshot of the gap between exports and imports of goods. With a large share of Canadian trade tied to the US, this is watched as a barometer of cross border demand and, indirectly, of how tariff related frictions are feeding through to the loonie.

The Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey, a measure of unfilled positions across the US economy that the Federal Reserve watches closely as a gauge of labour market slack. A drop toward pre pandemic levels would support the case for further Fed easing.

A broader measure of new orders placed with US manufacturers than the durable goods report released a few days earlier. Usually a secondary market mover, since much of the durable goods component is already known by the time this is published.

events.event: New Zealand employment change and unemployment rate (Q2)
events.description: Stats NZ's quarterly snapshot of the labour market, covering the change in the number of people employed and the jobless rate. A high reading for employment growth and a lower unemployment rate are both supportive for the New Zealand dollar; a weaker than expected set of figures would add to the case for the RBNZ to keep policy accommodative.

A private sector survey of activity in China's much larger services sector, released a few days after the manufacturing equivalent. Rounds out the picture from the official PMIs and the manufacturing Caixin print, with relevance for AUD and NZD given trade links to China.
The final, revised reading of S&P Global's Eurozone services survey. Usually only a small adjustment from the flash estimate, and a secondary mover for the euro compared with the manufacturing print.

The final, revised reading of S&P Global's UK services survey, covering the much larger part of the UK economy than manufacturing. Confirms or slightly adjusts the flash estimate published earlier in the month.

ADP's estimate of private sector payroll growth, released two days ahead of the official US jobs report. June's reading was a weak 57,000, well below forecasts, so this print will be watched closely for whether the labour market cooling flagged by Thursday's GDP miss is continuing.

The Institute for Supply Management's survey of the much larger US services sector, released on the third business day of the month. June's reading of 54.0 kept the sector in expansion for a 24th straight month; a reading above 50 signals growth, and this is one of the most closely watched US data points of the week.
